interactions.label: A 25-year-old medical student reports recurrent episodes of bilateral, band-like

params.question: A 25-year-old medical student reports recurrent episodes of bilateral, band-like tightness around the head, moderate in severity, without nausea, photophobia, or worsening with physical activity. Which primary headache syndrome is most consistent with this presentation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Migraine without aura is characterised by unilateral, pulsating pain of moderate-to-severe intensity with nausea and/or photophobia, worsened by routine physical activity — none of which are present here.

Correct. Bilateral, pressing or band-like quality, mild-to-moderate severity, and the absence of nausea or photophobia are the hallmarks of tension-type headache, distinguishing it clearly from migraine and cluster headache.

Cluster headache causes severe unilateral periorbital pain lasting up to three hours with ipsilateral autonomic features such as lacrimation, nasal congestion, and partial Horner syndrome — a very different profile.

Migraine with aura adds a fully reversible aura phase (typically a scintillating scotoma) before the headache. The underlying headache itself remains unilateral and pulsating with nausea, not bilateral and pressing.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three primary syndromes: migraine is unilateral and pulsating with nausea and photophobia; TTH is bilateral and pressing without nausea; cluster is severe periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic features.
Bilateral pressing pain without nausea is the signature of tension-type headache — the most common primary headache syndrome, accounting for the majority of primary headache consultations.

interactions.label: A normal non-contrast CT brain scan is sufficient to exclude subarachnoid haemor

params.question: A normal non-contrast CT brain scan is sufficient to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage in a patient with thunderclap headache.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A normal CT does not exclude SAH. The complete thunderclap protocol requires lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset when CT is normal. Missing this step carries catastrophic consequences — re-bleed risk within 24 hours is 20–30%, with a mortality of 40–50%.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. A normal CT does NOT exclude SAH. The thunderclap protocol requires both non-contrast CT AND lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset. Only when both are normal can SAH be excluded. Re-bleed risk within 24 hours is 20–30%, and missed re-bleed mortality is 40–50%.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old woman with known migraine reports that her headaches have changed

params.question: A 35-year-old woman with known migraine reports that her headaches have changed over the past month — they are now worst on waking and accompanied by projectile vomiting without preceding nausea. What should be the clinician's next step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Escalating prophylaxis assumes the old diagnosis still holds. A changed headache pattern in a known migraine patient must be treated as a new presentation requiring fresh workup.

answers.text: Investigate for raised intracranial pressure as a new diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Morning headache and effortless vomiting (without preceding nausea) are classic signs of raised intracranial pressure. When a known migraine patient describes a changed pattern, anchoring to the old label risks missing space-occupying lesions or venous sinus thrombosis.

answers.text: Advise a headache diary and review in four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying investigation when signs of raised ICP are present is dangerous. Morning headache with effortless vomiting demands urgent evaluation, not watchful waiting.

answers.text: Start a triptan for the acute episodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Triptans treat acute migraine attacks but do not address the underlying cause of a changed pattern. Effortless morning vomiting suggests raised ICP, which requires investigation, not symptomatic treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a known migraine patient's headache pattern changes, treat it as a new diagnosis. Morning headache and vomiting without nausea are classic raised ICP signs. Anchoring to the old label is how tumours and venous sinus thrombosis get missed.
A changed headache pattern always demands fresh investigation. Morning headache with effortless vomiting points to raised ICP — investigate before treating.

interactions.label: CSF analysis shows 150 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 70 mg/dL, and a CSF-to-serum glu

params.question: CSF analysis shows 150 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 70 mg/dL, and a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of 0.72. Which type of meningitis do these findings most strongly suggest?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial meningitis produces turbid, purulent fluid packed with neutrophils, protein above 100 mg/dL, and a glucose ratio below 0.4 — a completely different profile from the one described.

Correct. Lymphocytic pleocytosis with NORMAL glucose is the hallmark of viral meningitis. The preserved glucose ratio (0.72, well above 0.6) is the key separator from tuberculous meningitis, which shows a similar lymphocytic profile but with low glucose.

TB meningitis also shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, but characteristically has LOW glucose and higher protein elevation. The normal glucose ratio here is the key finding that argues against TB meningitis.

Cryptococcal meningitis typically shows few cells despite heavy infection, markedly raised opening pressure, and positive cryptococcal antigen — usually in immunocompromised patients with CD4 below 100.

overallFeedback.feedback: Both viral and TB meningitis show lymphocytic pleocytosis, but they diverge on glucose: viral preserves normal glucose (ratio above 0.6), while TB characteristically lowers it. This glucose distinction is the key separator.
Normal glucose with lymphocytic CSF points to viral meningitis. The glucose ratio is your most reliable discriminator when the cell profile looks similar to tuberculous meningitis.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old woman averaging six migraine attacks per month is also taking ibup

params.question: A 28-year-old woman averaging six migraine attacks per month is also taking ibuprofen on 18 days monthly. What must be done before starting preventive migraine therapy?

answers.text: Obtain an MRI brain to exclude secondary causes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Imaging is indicated only when red flags are present. The priority here is addressing the medication overuse that is perpetuating her chronic headache cycle.

answers.text: Switch her acute therapy from ibuprofen to sumatriptan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Switching the analgesic class does not solve the problem. Triptans carry the same medication-overuse risk when taken on ten or more days per month.

answers.text: Detoxify from medication overuse by reducing analgesic intake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Preventive therapy must be started only after medication-overuse headache detoxification. Anti-inflammatory drugs taken on 15 or more days monthly cause paradoxical worsening — the way out is reducing medication use, not escalating it.

answers.text: Start propranolol 40 mg daily alongside her current analgesic use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting prophylaxis before detoxification is ineffective. The ongoing medication overuse perpetuates the headache cycle and must be broken first before preventive therapy can work.

overallFeedback.feedback: Analgesics taken on 15 or more days monthly paradoxically worsen headaches. Preventive therapy cannot work until this overuse cycle is broken — detoxification must come first, not alongside or after prophylaxis.
Medication-overuse headache is the most underdiagnosed cause of chronic daily headache and is entirely iatrogenic. Always detoxify before starting preventive therapy.
